content: The treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) has evolved significantly, with the World Health Organization (WHO) providing updated guidelines to optimize patient outcomes. These guidelines emphasize the use of shorter, all-oral regimens and the inclusion of newer, more effective drugs while minimizing the use of toxic agents. 1. Six-Month BPaLM Regimen: WHO suggests a six-month treatment regimen consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid (600 mg), and moxifloxacin (BPaLM) for patients with MDR-TB or pre-extensively drug-resistant TB (pre-XDR-TB). This is preferred over longer regimens of 9 or 18 months. However, this recommendation is conditional due to very low certainty of evidence. 2. Nine-Month All-Oral Regimen: For patients with MDR-TB who do not have resistance to fluoroquinolones, WHO recommends a nine-month all-oral regimen instead of an 18-month regimen. This is also a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 3. Longer Regimens for MDR/RR-TB: For patients requiring longer regimens, WHO advises including all three Group A agents (bedaquiline, linezolid, and a fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin) and at least one Group B agent (clofazimine or cycloserine/terizidone). If only one or two Group A agents are used, both Group B agents should be included. Group C agents may be added if necessary to complete the regimen. Injectable agents like kanamycin and capreomycin should not be used. 4. Specific Drug Recommendations: Bedaquiline: Strongly recommended for patients aged 18 years or older on longer MDR-TB regimens. It may also be used in children aged 6–17 years and in all-oral regimens for children under 6 years, though these are conditional recommendations with very low certainty of evidence. Linezolid: Should be included in longer MDR-TB regimens. Delamanid: May be included in longer regimens for patients aged 3 years or older. For children under 3 years, it can be used as part of longer regimens. Clofazimine and Cycloserine/Terizidone: May be included in longer regimens. Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide: May be included in longer regimens. Imipenem-Cilastatin or Meropenem: May be included in longer regimens but must be administered with clavulanic acid, which is only available in combination with amoxicillin. Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is not counted as an additional effective TB agent. Amikacin: May be included in patients aged 18 years or older if susceptibility is demonstrated and adverse reactions can be monitored. Streptomycin may replace amikacin under the same conditions. Ethionamide/Prothionamide and p-Aminosalicylic Acid: These may only be included if better options are unavailable or if Group A and B agents are not used. Clavulanic Acid: Should not be included as a standalone agent in MDR-TB regimens. 5. Treatment Duration: For longer regimens, a total duration of 18–20 months is suggested for most patients, with adjustments based on the patient’s response to therapy. For regimens containing amikacin or streptomycin, an intensive phase of 6–7 months is suggested. 6. Monitoring and Adjunctive Therapies: Monthly sputum cultures are recommended in addition to smear microscopy to monitor treatment response. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated as early as possible (within the first 8 weeks) for all patients with HIV and drug-resistant TB, regardless of CD4 count. Elective partial lung resection (lobectomy or wedge resection) may be considered for patients with MDR-TB or rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) as part of a comprehensive treatment plan. 7. Rifampicin-Susceptible, Isoniazid-Resistant TB (Hr-TB): A six-month regimen of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin is recommended. Injectable agents like streptomycin should not be added to the treatment regimen. The WHO guidelines aim to improve treatment outcomes by incorporating evidence-based recommendations, reducing treatment duration, and minimizing the use of toxic drugs. These updates reflect advancements in TB management and the need for tailored approaches to address drug resistance patterns.
